content: 1. The calculation of retention rates differs from the focus on individuals lost to treatment, particularly among those newly initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) and those already on ART. This distinction is critical for program monitoring and implementing interventions aimed at improving retention in HIV care. It also facilitates tracing and re-engaging patients who have discontinued ART. 2. Updates to the HIV viral load (VL) monitoring algorithm recommend routine VL testing at six months after ART initiation (with samples collected earlier to ensure results are available at six months), at 12 months after ART initiation, and annually thereafter. This is essential for routine monitoring, assessing treatment success, and evaluating program effectiveness. 3. For HIV-positive pregnant women, VL testing is now recommended at 34–36 weeks of gestation (or at the latest, at delivery) to identify those at risk of treatment failure and/or perinatal transmission of HIV to their infants. 4. The role of CD4 cell count monitoring has evolved. CD4 testing should be performed at the first presentation to care and upon return to care after treatment interruption, especially in cases of high VL or advanced HIV disease. Routine CD4 testing for ART response monitoring can be discontinued in individuals with access to routine VL monitoring. However, periodic CD4 testing remains necessary for clinical management in cases of advanced HIV disease, clinical instability, or treatment interruption. 5. Systematic tuberculosis (TB) screening is now recommended at every visit for people living with HIV. This includes TB diagnosis using WHO-recommended molecular rapid diagnostic tests, HIV testing for individuals with confirmed or presumptive TB, and ART initiation within two weeks of starting TB treatment, regardless of CD4 count. Management of latent TB and shorter rifamycin-based TB preventive regimens are also emphasized. 6. A comprehensive package of interventions is recommended for individuals with advanced HIV disease. This includes screening, treatment, and/or prophylaxis for major opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and intensified adherence support interventions. 7. Patient monitoring systems should be updated to capture the implementation of these new guidelines, ensuring effective data collection and program evaluation. 8. HIV testing services (HTS) should be offered to all pregnant women and key populations, including testing for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) as early as possible. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are recommended as the first test in antenatal care (ANC) settings. 9. In high HIV burden settings, testing should be offered to all populations across various services, such as STI clinics, TB services, and maternal and child health services. In low HIV burden settings, testing should target individuals with clinical signs or conditions indicative of HIV, as well as key populations and their partners. 10. HIV self-testing (HIVST) is recommended as an additional approach to HIV testing, particularly in community-based settings, to enhance access and linkage to care. 11. Social network-based approaches can be utilized as part of a comprehensive HIV testing strategy for key populations, ensuring linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. 12. Retesting is critical in high HIV burden settings for sexually active individuals and those with ongoing HIV-related risks. It is also essential for individuals in prevention programs to confirm their HIV-negative status and ensure rapid linkage to ART in cases of seroconversion. 13. HIV patient monitoring systems, whether paper-based or electronic, should be updated to include comprehensive client data, facilitate linkage to care, and support person-centered HIV care across all service delivery points. 14. The guidelines emphasize the importance of harmonizing health data monitoring and reporting systems across program areas, including community-delivered services, to ensure effective integration and data flow. 15. At the facility level, healthcare providers and supervisors can use these guidelines to improve patient monitoring, retention, and health outcomes, as well as to enhance the quality of care and data use. 16. Program managers at subnational and national levels can utilize the guidance to analyze data, identify service delivery gaps, and improve the quality of care through targeted training and mentoring. 17. The guidelines do not address pharmacy services except for adherence and antiretroviral toxicity monitoring. They also do not include data elements for non-HIV-related TB care or maternal, newborn, and child health services. 18. Strategic information for HTS should be collected and analyzed using patient monitoring and routine program-based data to improve patient care and service delivery. 19. Standardized approaches to data collection and reporting are necessary across various testing settings and levels of healthcare facilities, including those integrating HTS into other clinical contexts like ANC and family planning. 20. Retesting is essential to ensure individuals in prevention programs remain HIV-negative and are promptly linked to ART if seroconversion occurs.
